children.author: alexjplant
children.text:
My friend and I played a round of golf with a random high school senior last week who spoke about how he was going to go to X college and get Y job to make Z dollars. For the first time in my life I truly felt old because I gave him the speech about how going to college in the US is more about where you go and who you meet than what you major in and your grades (as far as financial success in certain fields is concerned). Nobody explained this to me when I was younger. I heard a lot of "it's just a piece of paper you have to get out of the way" or "they're the best years of your life" or some variation thereof but never "you're going to get passed on for a job you're perfect for because you didn't go to Stanford/have a buddy/know a guy who knows a guy". I don't lose sleep over any of this because I couldn't have afforded to attend a name-brand school but I do wish I'd played things slightly differently.

As an aside: if you worked for Wikipedia I'd imagine that you're eminently employable.

My cousin went to Stanford, got a job at google (pre-IPO) and hasn't had to work a regular job for more than a decade.  I went to a state university, joined a few now-failed startups and worked for Wikipedia for 7 years. Now I'm living on my 401k, essentially unemployable.

Perhaps it means Variable Change?

When you agree to a price, you also agree to a change amount. The final amount paid gets the headline, but the true price and the change given back is kept on the down low. Where the change ends up going can also be disguised. It's like getting a massive kickback.

It's sort of like buying your own books to get on a best-seller list. The true sales amount is hidden, and the best-seller status garners even more sales.
